title: Magnify cell to 16F2 at F=40nm, magnify tiers to 120
idea: Deliberately enlarge the cell to 16F2 at a 40 nm half-pitch printable with dry ArF (no immersion, no EUV), then make it up in height by stacking 120 deposition-defined lateral-cell tiers, where each tier needs no new critical mask because only the deposition loop repeats. 16F2 at 40 nm is about 25,600 nm2 per tier, so 120 tiers gives roughly 4x the bit density of 6F2 at 12 nm.
why: Capital and litho wall: removes all 5-7 EUV layers and swaps them for repeated depositions, so depreciation per bit could drop by 2-3x while density still rises about 4x.

title: Minify tier thickness to 6 nm for 1000-tier atomic stacks
idea: Grow alternating MOCVD 2D-semiconductor channel sheets (MoS2 or WSe2, about 1 nm) and hBN/oxide spacers (about 5 nm) so each tier is 6 nm and 1000 tiers fit in a 6 um stack. Gain-cell storage nodes are gated by shared vertical gate holes etched once per 100-tier deck, as in 3D NAND.
why: 3D break-even (26+ tiers): goes 40x past it at a stack height that an etcher can already reach; the wide bandgap of 2D channels also cuts leakage, so refresh could fall by more than 100x.

title: Minify bitline to 16 cells with 2-transistor local preamp
idea: Cut each bitline into 16-cell segments. Each segment drives a global bitline through a 2-transistor local preamplifier, so the bitline capacitance seen by a cell falls from about 80 fF to about 3 fF. With that ratio, Cs can shrink from 5 fF to about 0.5 fF, and the capacitor becomes a shallow planar or low-AR cup instead of a 70:1 pillar.
why: Capacitor charge wall: Cs needed drops by 10x, removing the need for AR 115 or k 70. Area overhead is about 12%, against much cheaper capacitor process steps.

title: Magnify bitline to 4096 cells using current-read gain cells
idea: In a vertical-bitline 3D array, hang 4096 tiered 3T gain cells on one bitline. They are read non-destructively by current, not by charge sharing, so bitline capacitance no longer limits signal and one sense amp serves 8x more cells than in 1T1C.
why: Periphery takes 49% of the die: sense-amp and bitline-driver area per bit falls by about 8x, which could free 25-30% of die area for cells.

title: Minify the page to 64 bits with AND-gated wordline slices
idea: Split each wordline into 64-bit slices, each with a local AND gate that combines the row decode with a column-group select, so a random 64B access fires only 512 cells instead of 8 KB of cells.
why: 128x overfetch and the 5.9 pJ per useful bit of a random read: activation energy per useful bit could fall by 10-16x, and row-hammer disturbance is limited to the active slice.

title: Magnify wafer use: double-sided cells around a mid-height bitline
idea: Bury the bitline at mid-height in the wafer. An upper vertical transistor and capacitor are built on the front side; after bonding and thinning, a second vertical transistor and capacitor are built on the backside, both hanging from the same bitline. Two storage cells then share each 4F2 footprint, for 2F2 effective.
why: Density and litho: doubles bits per mm2 without a smaller F, so the same EUV layer count buys about 2x the bits.

title: Minify front-side clutter: move 4F2 bitlines to wafer backside
idea: In a vertical-channel 4F2 cell, form the bitlines on the backside after wafer thinning to about 300 nm, contacting the bottom of each vertical channel, as backside power delivery does. The front side is then free for a full-height capacitor, and the buried-bitline coupling and resistance problem goes away.
why: Makes 4F2 manufacturable: 33% less area than 6F2, lower BL-BL coupling (about 30% less sense noise), and a wider BL metal (about 3x lower resistance).

title: Magnify access gate length 10x using free vertical space
idea: Since 3D arrays have spare height, make the vertical gate-all-around access channel about 300 nm long with a 5 nm thin body, instead of a short planar or recessed channel. This suppresses short-channel and DIBL leakage paths that create the 13 fA tail.
why: Refresh: a tighter leakage tail could stretch retention about 10x (64 ms to about 640 ms), cutting refresh energy and bandwidth loss by about 90%.

title: Magnify capacitor AR to 300:1 with wet metal-assisted chemical etching
idea: Form the storage capacitor as a deep trench in the substrate using metal-assisted chemical etching, where gold or silver catalyst dots sink into Si in an HF/H2O2 bath to give AR above 300:1 with no plasma etcher. A vertical access transistor sits on top, reviving trench-capacitor DRAM.
why: Charge wall: Cs could reach about 15-20 fF at the same footprint, with a cheap wet bench instead of $50M+ high-AR plasma etchers.

title: Magnify capacitor height with three stacked 40:1 decks
idea: Build the capacitor mold in three decks, each AR about 40 (easy to etch), joined by self-aligned landing plugs, borrowing the multi-deck channel-hole method of 3D NAND. The total effective AR is about 120.
why: Charge wall: reaches the AR about 115 that higher Cs requires using existing etchers. Cs rises about 1.6x, which could relax VARY or extend retention.

title: Magnify capacitor sidewall area 2.5x with corrugated superlattice mold
idea: Deposit the capacitor mold as an alternating SiN/SiO2 (or Si/SiGe) superlattice, etch the hole, then selectively recess every other layer, so the pillar sidewall becomes a corrugated bellows that the ALD electrode and dielectric coat conformally.
why: Charge wall: about 2.5x more electrode area, and so Cs, at the same AR of 60-75. This could avoid the jump to AR 115.

title: Minify temperature to 77 K, minify capacitor to 0.5 fF
idea: Run whole memory sleds immersed in liquid nitrogen. At 77 K, junction and subthreshold leakage fall by more than six orders of magnitude, so a planar 0.5 fF capacitor holds data for hours, and a 4F2 cell needs no high-AR pillar at all.
why: Capacitor wall and refresh: refresh disappears, the capacitor process collapses to planar, and density could reach about 1.5x 6F2. The cost is cryocooling at datacenter scale.

title: Magnify die to the full wafer: wafer-scale DRAM
idea: Make a 300 mm wafer one memory, with no dicing: tiles are linked by an on-wafer mesh with spare-tile rerouting. Bond it face-to-face to a wafer-scale compute wafer, so there are no packages, PHYs or scribe lines.
why: Data movement and packaging: about 1 TB per wafer pair at about 0.1 pJ/bit, recovering about 5-8% of wafer area lost to scribe lines and edges.

title: Minify DRAM die to 0.5 mm2 confetti, self-assembled onto logic
idea: Make DRAM as tiny 0.5 mm2 micro-dies, whose small area gives near-100% yield, and deposit thousands at once onto logic wafers by fluidic self-assembly into shaped receptor wells, followed by hybrid bonding.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield: avoids the 20-30% stack yield loss and the 3x area per bit, with a microLED-style mass-transfer cost.

title: Magnify sharing: eight array-only wafers on one periphery wafer
idea: Bond eight array-only wafers (cells, wordlines and bitlines; about 4 masks each, no periphery) onto one CMOS periphery wafer. Nano-TSV global bitline risers and a tier-select transistor let each sense amp serve all eight tiers.
why: Periphery takes 49% of the die: periphery area per bit falls 8x, and array wafers drop most critical and periphery masks.

title: Magnify row spacing: spend 3D density on grounded shield wordlines
idea: In a stacked array where density is abundant, insert a grounded shield wordline between every pair of active wordlines and a shield plane between tiers, so aggressor-victim capacitive and charge-migration coupling falls sharply.
why: Row hammer: the flip threshold could rise from about 1k to about 100k activations, removing costly TRR and RFM overheads for about 30% of area.

title: Magnify redundancy to 30% spare tiers with boot-time self-repair
idea: Design 3D DRAM with about 30% spare tiers and rows, plus a built-in self-test that remaps failing rows at every power-on, so a stack can tolerate a defect density about 10x higher than 2D DRAM.
why: Unlocks a 3D manufacturing cell that is not yet manufacturable: cheaper, less perfect deposition could ship sooner at about 70% usable density.

title: Minify tunnel oxide to 1.5 nm: leaky 3D NAND as DRAM
idea: Take a 200+ layer charge-trap 3D NAND flow and thin the tunnel oxide to about 1.5 nm, so cells write by direct tunneling in about 10-50 ns and leak in about 1-10 s. The controller refreshes them like DRAM, and direct tunneling may avoid hot-carrier wear.
why: Reuses the cheapest per-bit 3D process in the world for working memory, with density about 5-10x DRAM. Endurance is unproven.

title: Minify litho to zero EUV: block-copolymer hex-lattice 4F2
idea: Let block-copolymer cylinders self-assemble into a hexagonal lattice at about 24 nm pitch, guided by one coarse DUV template, to define the vertical-channel pillars and caps of a hexagonal 4F2 array.
why: Litho capital: could replace 3-5 EUV layers with a spin-coat and bake, cutting array patterning cost about 5x.

title: Minify the data path: each mat bonds straight down to logic
idea: Hybrid-bond every DRAM mat's local I/O directly to the logic die below at 1-2 um pitch, removing global datalines and the PHY, for a 65,536-bit-wide interface at about 250 MHz.
why: Data movement and periphery: I/O energy could fall from 3-4 pJ/bit to about 0.05-0.1 pJ/bit, and global bus area drops about 10% of the die.

title: Minify speed to 1 us: 2-bit cells with shared ramp sensing
idea: Build a deliberately slow far-memory tier with 1 us access: cells store 2 bits (4 charge levels), and 64 bitlines share one slow, precise ramp-ADC sense circuit, time-multiplexed.
why: Cost per bit: 2x bits per cell and 64x fewer sense amps, for tiered memory holding cold KV-cache and pages at about 40-50% lower cost per bit.

title: Minify die to 4 um thick: 64-high nano-TSV stack
idea: Use wafer-on-wafer bonding and grind each DRAM wafer to an etch stop at about 4 um, then link layers with 0.5 um nano-TSVs instead of 40 um microbumps, stacking 64 dies in about 300 um.
why: HBM TSV tax: TSV keep-out area could fall 10-50x and stack height capacity rise 4-5x.

title: Magnify cells per transistor: vertical CCD shift-register string
idea: Stack 8 storage nodes along one vertical channel and clock the tier gates as CCD phases, so charge packets shift down bucket-brigade style to a single access transistor and sense node at the bottom. This is 1970s planar CCD memory turned 3D.
why: Density and the access-transistor problem: 8 bits per access device and bitline contact, cutting 3D transistor count about 8x, with serial latency of about 20-40 ns.

title: Magnify AR with a beaker: anodic alumina capacitors over logic
idea: On a $150k 28 nm MPW die, deposit aluminium in the BEOL and anodize it into self-ordered pores (about 65 nm pitch, AR above 100), then ALD-line them. Each cell's landing pad captures about 8 random pores, so no pore-to-transistor registration is needed. Demonstrate a 10 fF-per-cell capacitor-over-logic DRAM macro in a university cleanroom within 18 months.
why: Charge wall and capital: high-AR capacitors made electrochemically at room temperature, with no high-AR etcher. The prototype fits easily inside $1M.

title: Minify staircase contacts: in-tier pass-gate decoders
idea: Build log2(N) pass-gate decoder trees from the same lateral access transistors inside each 3D tier, so the staircase needs about log2 of the per-tier wordline contacts instead of one per row. Validate with TCAD, a 4-tier coupon and a patent package, then license.
why: 3D DRAM blocker: staircase and contact area per tier could fall about 10x, lowering the 26-tier break-even point. Design plus coupon costs about $600k.

title: Minify the 3D demo: 4-tier Si/SiGe cells on 100 mm coupons
idea: Buy commercial Si/SiGe superlattice epitaxy wafers (about $5-10k each), then in a rented university cleanroom selectively remove SiGe, ALD gate and capacitor stacks, and demonstrate a 4-tier lateral-channel 1T1C cell with retention data in 18 months.
why: A credible 3D cell data point that de-risks licensing or fundraising for about $400k, against vendor 3D programs costing billions.

title: Magnify yield: stitch rejected DRAM dies into good ones
idea: Buy partially failing or downbinned DRAM dies at scrap prices, then pair three partial dies under a small remap and sparing logic die (FPGA first, then a $100k MPW ASIC) that presents one fully good logical die in a stacked package.
why: Scarce supply: turns DRAM yield fallout (a few % of output) into sellable capacity at about 30-50% of contract price, with no fab.

title: Magnify usable bits: reclaim on-die ECC parity cells
idea: DDR5 dies carry about 6.25% extra cells for on-die ECC. Partner with a second-tier vendor to expose a test-mode map that releases those cells as user capacity for error-tolerant data such as AI weights and caches, with protection handled by host-side ECC.
why: Supply: about 6% more usable bits from every die already built. Only firmware, characterization and a vendor deal are needed, about $500k.

title: Minify TSVs to zero: print staircase stack interconnects
idea: Offset 16 commodity bare LPDDR dies into a staircase and aerosol-jet print fine sidewall traces down each step to a substrate, giving a tall, TSV-free stack built in a packaging lab for about $300k.
why: HBM TSV tax: more capacity per package without the 3x wafer area or the 20-30% TSV yield hit, using dies that can be bought today.

title: Magnify coil count, minify TSVs: inductive-coupled die stack
idea: Tape out a $100k 40 nm MPW chip with thousands of top-metal micro-coils as through-chip wireless links, then thin and glue-stack 8 dies with no TSVs to prove the bandwidth, energy per bit and yield gain.
why: HBM TSV tax: removes TSV area and the drilling yield loss. Proves inter-die links below 1 pJ/bit within budget.

title: Magnify threshold during hold with FD-SOI back-gate bias
idea: Design a 1T1C or 2T cell on a 22 nm FD-SOI MPW in which the back gate swings to about -2 V during hold to raise the access transistor's Vt and cut leakage about 1000x, then returns to 0 V for fast access.
why: Refresh: retention moves from ms toward seconds on a commercial process with no new materials. Test chip and characterization cost about $400k.

title: Minify bitline noise: helical twisted bitlines across tiers
idea: In a 3D vertical-bitline array, route bitline pairs so they swap tier positions every 16 cells, forming a helix that cancels BL-BL coupling noise. Prove it with SPICE and extracted parasitics plus a small 130 nm MPW test array.
why: Charge wall: lower noise lets sense margin, and so Cs, shrink by about 20-30%. A design-only path licenses it for under $400k.

title: Minify sense-amp offset by trimming each amp after fab
idea: Add a fuse- or antifuse-programmed binary capacitor trim to every sense-amp pair, set during wafer test, to cancel measured offset below 5 mV. Prove it on a 28 nm MPW and license to second-tier DRAM makers.
why: Charge wall: smaller offset allows about 30% smaller Cs or lower VARY. The IP plus test chip fits in $1M.

title: Magnify effective capacity: compression engine in the base die
idea: Prototype a stack whose logic base die compresses cache lines inline, with 64B lines packed into variable slots by a metadata table, using an FPGA in front of commodity DRAM. Then tape out the engine as a $200k chiplet.
why: Supply: about 1.5-2x effective capacity on compressible AI and server data from the same DRAM bits.

title: Magnify the 3D array 20x to measure parasitics cheaply
idea: Build 3D tier stacks at 20x feature size with contact lithography but identical aspect ratios and materials, and measure their tier-to-tier and BL-BL coupling and RC directly. Calibrate 3D DRAM design models for about $150k.
why: Speeds up 3D array design: capacitive coupling scales geometrically, so a cheap magnified twin gives real parasitic data years before nm tiers exist.

title: Minify substrate, magnify layers: fold one memory sheet 32 times
idea: Make one long thin-film memory array on 10 um polyimide through a flexible-TFT foundry shuttle, then fold it accordion-style 32 times, with fold lines carrying edge interconnects to a controller.
why: Layer count by folding instead of tier deposition: tests a no-bonding 3D path for under $300k. Density per layer is low, so it is a moonshot demo.

title: Minify the fab: iterate 3D tiers on half-inch-wafer tools
idea: Rent time on half-inch-wafer minimal-fab tool sets, about 1/1000 the capex of a 300 mm line with cycle times of days, to run hundreds of 3D DRAM tier process splits (deposition, selective recess, ALD) in 24 months.
why: Capital and time: turns 3D cell R&D from a $100M problem into a budget below $1M, with 10x more learning cycles.

title: Magnify contributors: open-source 3D DRAM compiler and PDK
idea: Fund three engineers to release an open-source array generator for SKY130 and GF180, plus a parametric 3D DRAM tier model (tier count, Cs, leakage tail, spares) and a cost and yield calculator, so universities can tape out DRAM arrays on open shuttles.
why: U.S. manufacturability and talent: brings hundreds of designers to array architecture for about $900k.

title: Minify the cost of discovery: an 8-tier DRAM inducement prize
idea: Put up a $400k prize, verified at a neutral university lab, for the first open demonstration of a stack of at least 8 tiers with at least 1 fF per cell and 64 ms retention. The winner grants the sponsor a licensing option.
why: 3D DRAM blocker: buys many parallel attempts for the price of one engineer team.

title: Minify rank width: one-chip sub-rank access controller
idea: Build an FPGA DIMM controller that addresses each x4 DDR5 chip independently through per-chip command buffering, so a random access activates one chip's row instead of 8-16 chips' rows.
why: Overfetch: random-access activation energy (graph, KV cache) could fall about 8x on existing DIMMs. The FPGA prototype costs about $250k.

title: Minify transferred tier to 30 nm: ion-cut two-tier 1T1C
idea: Use vendor Smart Cut SOI services to bond and transfer a 30 nm single-crystal Si film onto a first finished cell tier, then build the second tier below 450 C with laser anneal in a university fab, proving 2-tier monolithic 1T1C for about $500k.
why: 3D integration: single-crystal tiers, with better leakage than poly or oxide channels, and no per-tier wafer bonding at cell pitch.

title: Magnify bus width 8x on a cheap glass interposer
idea: Place four bare commodity LPDDR dies side by side on a panel-made glass interposer with 2 um lines, giving a 1024-bit bus to an FPGA or ASIC without TSVs or a silicon interposer, built through glass-panel vendors for about $300k.
why: HBM TSV tax: HBM-like bandwidth from LPDDR bits, without HBM's 3x wafer area per bit or stack yield loss.

title: Magnify old ideas: buy dormant trench-capacitor DRAM IP
idea: Acquire dormant legacy trench-capacitor DRAM patents and design data at distressed prices, then adapt the deep-trench array to a U.S. specialty foundry's existing deep-trench module for a niche legacy-DRAM product.
why: U.S. manufacturability: a DRAM path with no stacked-capacitor etch or EUV. The IP plus feasibility study fit under $1M.

title: Minify litho capex: nanoimprint a 4F2 hex array
idea: Commission one $100k nanoimprint master of a hexagonal 4F2 pillar array at about 20 nm pitch and replicate it on coupons with a rented NIL tool, proving pattern fidelity and overlay for the cell layer.
why: Litho capital: one stamp could replace multiple EUV exposures for the regular cell array, about 5-10x cheaper per layer.

title: Minify refresh by die position: per-die refresh in HBM stacks
idea: On an FPGA-with-HBM board, measure how retention varies with each die's position in the stack, then have a custom controller issue per-channel refresh at rates matched to each die's measured temperature and retention rather than the hottest die.
why: Refresh in 3D stacks: could cut refresh by about 30-40% on cooler dies, using firmware and controller IP that cost about $300k.

title: Minify TSV count 4x with PAM-4 and time-multiplexed vias
idea: Design TSV transceivers that send PAM-4 at 2x the symbol rate, with 2:1 time-multiplexing, so a quarter of the TSVs carry the same bandwidth. Validate on a TSV interposer MPW and license to stack makers.
why: HBM TSV tax: TSV keep-out area and drilling yield loss could fall about 4x. The test vehicle costs about $500k.
